name: Pseudocertainty effect
statement: An outcome that depends on clearing an earlier uncertain stage is treated as though it were guaranteed, so it beats an identical option stated as a flat probability.
meaning: Two gambles can be identical in their final outcomes and probabilities and still be described in ways that produce opposite choices. Put the choice inside a game with a preliminary stage that both options share, and the second-stage prize starts to feel like a sure thing. It is not one, because reaching the second stage is itself uncertain. Tversky and Kahneman proposed that people evaluate the problem conditionally, as if the first stage had already been cleared, which deletes the shared contingency from the calculation. The same trick works through causal contingencies rather than a sequence of stages, by naming a specific hazard the option fully covers and leaving the rest of the risk unmentioned. Insurance is the standing example. Cover against fire but not flood can be read either as complete protection against fire or as a partial cut in the chance of losing the house, and the two readings do not rank it the same way.

origin.note: The name appears in "The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice", in a section on the framing of contingencies covering problems 5 to 7. The demonstration is older than the name. Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 prospect theory paper ran the same two-stage game as Problem 10 and filed it under the isolation effect, alongside a second demonstration about outcomes that the 1981 name does not cover.

evidence: Tversky and Kahneman put three problems to separate groups of students at Stanford University and the University of British Columbia. Each group was told that one respondent in ten, chosen at random, would play for money, with chance events settled in the room by drawing a ball from a bag and winners paid on the spot. Problem 5 offered a sure win of $30 against an 80 per cent chance of $45, and 78 per cent of 77 respondents took the sure $30. Problem 6 wrapped the identical second-stage choice in a game with a 75 per cent chance of ending at stage one with nothing, and required the choice before the first stage was resolved. There, 74 per cent of 85 respondents took the $30. Problem 7 stated the same two prospects as flat probabilities, a 25 per cent chance of $30 against a 20 per cent chance of $45, and 58 per cent of 81 respondents took the $45. Problems 6 and 7 are the same gamble, since 0.25 times 0.80 is 0.20. The 1979 pair ran larger and in Israeli pounds. Of 95 respondents given the flat version, 65 per cent chose the 20 per cent chance of 4,000 over a 25 per cent chance of 3,000; of 141 given the two-stage version, 78 per cent chose the 3,000. Tversky and Kahneman also report a version with lives. Respondents were told that risk to life arose only if the disease was carried by one particular virus, with probability .10. Two programmes were said to give a sure loss of 75 lives or an 80 per cent chance of losing 100 lives if that virus was involved. The real choice was between a 10 per cent chance of losing 75 lives and an 8 per cent chance of losing 100, and preferences matched the unconditional version. The paper further cites an unpublished study by Paul Slovic, Baruch Fischhoff and Sarah Lichtenstein. A vaccine cutting the chance of a disease from .20 to .10 was less attractive described as effective in half of cases than as fully effective against one of two equally likely strains with identical symptoms. No figures for that study are given in the 1981 paper or in Kahneman and Tversky's 1984 restatement of it.

replication.headline: A preregistered study in 19 countries reran the 1979 two-stage game and the gap held, though the plain-probability half of the pair has drifted to a coin flip since 1979.
replication.detail: Ruggeri and 31 colleagues put 17 of the 20 items from Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper to 4,098 people in 19 countries and 13 languages, converting values to local currency and preregistering the analysis at osf.io/esxc4. Their item 11 is the two-stage game and their item 4 is the flat-probability equivalent, and the contrast between them is the paper's single test of the isolation effect. It was one of the 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts that replicated, with a Z statistic of 31.72 and p below 0.0001, and it was one of only four contrasts with no significant between-country heterogeneity, Q(18) = 19.39, p = 0.3681, I-squared = 0. The flat item is the half that moved. Its pooled estimate is 0.51, with a 95 per cent CI of 0.48 to 0.54 and p = 0.54, so it cannot be told apart from chance, against 65 per cent choosing the gamble in 1979. The article prints no pooled proportion for the two-stage item, which appears only in a figure. A supplementary analysis trimmed to the 1979 sample sizes puts the pair at 17 and 52 per cent against 22 and 65 per cent in 1979, and the authors kept that analysis out of the final manuscript. The Bulgarian team ran Fisher's exact test on the same two items and report an odds ratio of 0.20, 95 per cent CI 0.05 to 0.66, p = 0.0036, which they read as people being five times likelier to answer the two differently than alike. Millroth, Nilsson and Juslin ran a conceptual replication of the same 1979 items on 346 people in a within-subject design and 1,287 in a single-stimuli design, recruited online in the United States and scored on the four-item Berlin Numeracy Test. Pooled, the two proportions sit far apart: 16.3 per cent chose the gamble in the two-stage item, 95 per cent credible interval 13.1 to 20.2, against 44.1 per cent in the flat item, 39.4 to 48.8, with a Bayes factor above 1,000 against the two being equal. Their own scoring is harsher than that gap suggests. They count a paradox as replicated only where the two modal choices match 1979, and their flat item's majority took the 3,000 prospect rather than the gamble, the opposite of the original. On that test the isolation effect for probabilities failed at every numeracy level but the highest. Counted per person rather than per group, the paradox is a minority pattern. It appeared in 38 per cent of the 346 within-subject respondents, rising from 28 per cent of the 130 who scored zero on the numeracy test to 75 per cent of the 8 who scored four.

study.cite: Ruggeri, K., Alí, S., Berge, M. L., et al. (2020). Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk. Nature Human Behaviour, 4(6), 622-633.

limits: What has been repeated is the 1979 two-stage game, not the 1981 problems the name was coined for. Crossref, Europe PMC and an open-web search on 21 September 2026 found no replication of Tversky and Kahneman's problems 5 to 7, of the epidemic-virus version, or of the Slovic, Fischhoff and Lichtenstein vaccine framing. OpenAlex refused every query that day with a rate-limit status and is not among the venues searched. Kahneman and Tversky reprinted the two-stage pair in 1984 with the same samples and the same percentages, which is a restatement and not a second test. The 1981 problems are also the versions with real money behind them, at odds of one in ten, and both large modern tests pay nothing for the choice itself. The vaccine study is a further gap. It is cited as unpublished in 1981 and as Slovic, Fischhoff and Lichtenstein 1982 in Kahneman and Tversky's later account, and neither source prints a sample size or a proportion for it, so the description above is all there is. The chapter itself was not obtained. Two cautions apply to the modern pair. Ruggeri and colleagues treat the contrast as a test of the isolation effect, which is the wider 1979 category, and the 1979 isolation demonstration about outcomes is not part of this entry. They also dropped three of the 1979 items, including the probabilistic insurance question, as too wordy for a study in 13 languages. Millroth and colleagues' numeracy gradient rests on thin cells at the top: the group scoring four out of four on the Berlin Numeracy Test held 8 people in the within-subject sample, and their confidence intervals are correspondingly wide. Their study is described by its authors as a conceptual rather than a direct replication.
misreadings: The certainty effect and the pseudocertainty effect are different claims and the 1981 paper separates them. The certainty effect compares a genuinely sure prize with a merely probable one, and the two options really do differ in probability. What it violates is the substitution axiom, an assumption about attitudes to risk. Pseudocertainty compares two descriptions of one gamble in which nothing is certain in either. What it violates is the requirement that preferences not depend on how a problem is written, which Tversky and Kahneman called the more fundamental of the two. The certainty effect has its own entry at no. 185. The two are not measured together here. Tversky and Kahneman read the certainty effect off problems 5 and 7 and the pseudocertainty effect off problems 6 and 7, and Ruggeri and colleagues keep the certainty contrasts and the isolation contrast apart in the same way. The framing effect is the closer relative and still not the same thing. In the Asian disease problem the probabilities are held fixed and the wording of the outcomes changes, moving the reference point so that saved lives become deaths. In the two-stage game the outcomes are described identically and in one valence, and what changes is the contingency structure. Tversky and Kahneman keep the two apart in the paper. The disease pair opens it, as the first illustration of framing, and problems 5 to 7 come later under the framing of contingencies. The second common error is treating the result as a claim about individuals. Both modern tests measure a difference between group proportions, and the one that counted per person found the pattern in 38 per cent of respondents. The third is reading pseudocertainty into probabilistic insurance, which is a nearby finding about disliking cover that might not pay out. Millroth and colleagues tested that one as a separate item. Ruggeri and colleagues left it out of their survey altogether. Finally, the effect is often described as people preferring certainty. What the two-stage game shows is people ignoring a stage whose outcome is the same whichever option they pick, and certainty is what that deletion leaves behind.

Problems 5, 6 and 7 and the epidemic-virus variant are in the section "The Framing of Contingencies". Read on 21 September 2026 from the JSTOR scan posted by Hanover College, the publisher's own copy being closed. Every problem, percentage, sample size and procedural detail quoted above was checked in it.

Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263-291. Problem 10 is the two-stage game; Problem 4 is its flat-probability equivalent, in Table I. Read on 21 September 2026 from the copy posted at MIT; the two sample sizes and both percentages were checked in it, as was the currency.

Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1984). Choices, values, and frames. American Psychologist, 39(4), 341-350. Restates the vaccine study and attributes it to Slovic, Fischhoff and Lichtenstein (1982), without figures. Read on 21 September 2026 from the University of Miami copy. It also reprints the two-stage pair as its problems 5 and 6, with the 1981 samples and percentages unchanged, and it does not use the name.
